etymology: Hebrew Maakathi (H4602), an inhabitant of Maachah, a small Aramean kingdom at the foot of mount Hermon on the north-eastern border of Israel's inheritance.
biblical_def: The Maachathites were a people of the small Syrian kingdom of Maachah, lying beneath Hermon on the edge of Bashan (Jos 12:5). Their land fell within the territory allotted to Israel when Og was defeated, and Joshua records what happened next with painful brevity: Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day (Jos 13:13). The command had been plain and the victory had been given; the tribes simply stopped short. Two later notices show the consequence quietly at work. One of David's thirty is Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite (2Sa 23:34), the blood already mingled; and at the very end of the kingdom, among the captains who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after Jerusalem fell, is Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite (2Ki 25:23). The people Israel did not drive out were still there, inside the story, from the conquest to the captivity.
webster_summary: An inhabitant of Maachah, a Syrian kingdom below mount Hermon, whom Israel failed to expel from the allotted inheritance.

And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.
corruption_summary: Incomplete obedience is counted as substantial success; Joshua records the tribes' unfinished conquest as the seed of everything that followed.
corruption_paragraphs: The book of Joshua is usually remembered for its victories, and the refrain that runs underneath them is easy to miss: they expelled not. Judah could not drive out the Jebusites; Ephraim drave not out the Canaanites of Gezer; Manasseh did not; Zebulun did not; Asher did not; Naphtali did not; and the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites nor the Maachathites. Each notice is small and reasonable-sounding — the enemy was strong, had chariots of iron, could be put to tribute. Together they are the hinge on which the book of Judges turns, and the LORD's messenger says so outright: they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you (Jdg 2:3).

The application is not to land but to sin, and Scripture makes it directly. The believer is commanded to mortify, to put off, to cut off, to make no provision for the flesh — and the besetting sin left standing because it seemed manageable is the one that furnishes the next generation's idolatry. Owen's rule holds: sin not mortified is sin gathering strength. The principle to recover is that partial obedience is a form of disobedience with a better reputation, and that the thing a man does not drive out will still be living in his house when his grandchildren are grown.

etymology: Hebrew Naamathi (H5284), an inhabitant of Naamah, a place otherwise unknown; the root naem (H5276) means to be pleasant or agreeable.
biblical_def: The word occurs four times in Scripture and always of one man: Zophar the Naamathite, the third of Job's three friends. He came with Eliphaz and Bildad when they heard of all the evil that had come upon Job, for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him (Job 2:11), and they began well — seven days and seven nights on the ground beside him, and none spake a word. Then the speeches began. Zophar speaks twice (Job 11 and 20), and he is the harshest of the three: he tells Job that God exacts of him less than his iniquity deserves, and devotes a whole chapter to the short triumphing of the wicked. He does not speak a third time; the argument runs out. At the end the LORD's verdict falls on all three: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath (Job 42:7), and they were commanded to bring a burnt offering and let Job pray for them — and the LORD also accepted Job (Job 42:9).
webster_summary: An inhabitant of Naamah; in Scripture always the designation of Zophar, the third of Job's three friends.

corruption_summary: Suffering is read as a reliable index of guilt; the book of Job exists to refute that reading, and God rebukes the men who made it.
corruption_paragraphs: Zophar's theology is not exotic. It is the ordinary retribution principle held rigidly: God is just, God governs, therefore the man in ashes has earned his ashes. It is the same reasoning the disciples brought to the blind man — who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? — and the Lord Jesus answered Neither (Joh 9:2-3). He said the same about the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices, and the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell: they were not sinners above all others (Luk 13:1-5). The book of Job is in the canon largely to kill this inference, and it kills it by telling the reader in chapter one what none of the characters know.

The modern form of the error is the prosperity teaching in reverse: if a believer is sick, poor or crushed, some hidden fault must account for it — unconfessed sin, a lack of faith, a wrong confession. The counsel that follows is Zophar's counsel in a softer accent, and it does the same damage. The principle to recover is the one God vindicated: a man may be upright, may fear God and eschew evil, and may still be broken; and the friends who came to comfort him ended up needing him to pray for them. Sit on the ground for seven days if necessary, and be very slow to explain another man's affliction to him.

etymology: Hebrew Shuchi (H7747), a descendant of Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:2), whose people settled east of Canaan among the Arabian tribes.
biblical_def: The word belongs in Scripture to Bildad the Shuhite, the second of Job's three friends, and it occurs five times, always attached to him (Job 2:11; 8:1; 18:1; 25:1; 42:9). His descent from Shuah, Abraham's son by Keturah, places the whole book in the patriarchal world east of Canaan, among peoples who had some knowledge of the true God without the law of Moses. Bildad's distinctive argument is the appeal to antiquity: Enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers… shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart? (Job 8:8-10). He is the traditionalist of the three, and he uses the tradition to press the same conclusion the others press — that Job's children died for their transgression and that God does not cast away a perfect man. His last speech is six verses long, and the argument collapses. At the end he stood with the others under the same rebuke and brought the same burnt offering.
webster_summary: A descendant of Shuah the son of Abraham by Keturah; in Scripture the designation of Bildad, the second of Job's three friends.

corruption_summary: Tradition is treated as self-authenticating; Bildad's appeal to the fathers was sincere, venerable, and wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: Bildad's method deserves a careful verdict, because it is half right. Enquire of the former age… shall not they teach thee? is sound instinct. The accumulated wisdom of godly generations is a real gift, and a man who despises it will repeat every error the church has already paid for. This dictionary confesses subordinate standards for exactly that reason, and honours the Reformers and the Puritans as faithful witnesses. The trouble is what Bildad did with the inheritance: he made it the final court, and used it to crush a man whose case the tradition had not anticipated.

Scripture sets the order and never varies it. Confessions and fathers are subordinate standards, binding for the church that receives them but always under Scripture; the Bereans were commended for searching the scriptures daily to see whether even apostolic preaching was so (Act 17:11); and the Lord Jesus condemned teaching for doctrines the commandments of men (Mat 15:9). Rome's error is to raise tradition to the level of Scripture; the sectarian error is to despise it altogether. The principle to recover is the Reformed middle: receive the fathers gratefully, test them relentlessly, and never let a venerable formula silence a text or crush a sufferer it was never written to address.

etymology: Hebrew Harari (H2043), mountaineer or man of the hill country — from har (H2022), a mountain, a hill.
biblical_def: Hararite is the designation of three of David's mighty men, and one of them gives the word its meaning. After him was Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. And the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people fled from the Philistines (2Sa 23:11). The next verse finishes it: Shammah stood in the midst of the ground, defended it, slew the Philistines, and the LORD wrought a great victory. A field of lentils is not a strategic asset. It is a poor man's dinner, and everyone else had already decided it was not worth dying for. The other Hararites are Ahiam the son of Sharar (2Sa 23:33) and Jonathan the son of Shage (1Ch 11:34), both of the same hill-country stock. The name means mountaineer, and it fits the men: hill people who did not run downhill. Scripture keeps the lentil field in the record on purpose, because the question it puts is the useful one — not whether a man would die for something obviously great, but whether he will hold the small ground God gave him when everybody else has gone.
webster_summary: A mountaineer, a man of the hill country; the designation of three of David's mighty men, chief among them Shammah who defended a field of lentiles.

corruption_summary: Faithfulness is imagined as a matter of great occasions; the mighty men are remembered for holding ground nobody thought worth holding.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Hararites are uncontested. What their chapter contests is a persistent fantasy about courage — that it waits for a cause large enough to deserve it, and that the ordinary ground a man stands on is too small to matter. Shammah's field was full of lentils. The people fled, and by every reasonable calculation they were right: a bean patch is not worth a life.

Scripture disagrees, and records that the LORD wrought a great victory over it. The reason is that the field was Israel's, and yielding it was yielding covenant ground to the Philistines, whatever the crop. The same logic runs through the New Testament's treatment of small fidelity: he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luk 16:10), and the servant commended is commended for having been faithful over a few things (Mat 25:21). The principle to recover is that most Christian courage is exercised over unimpressive ground — a marriage, a doctrine nobody else is defending, a job done honestly when no one checks — and the LORD counts a lentil field held as a great victory.

etymology: Hebrew Yithri (H3505), a member of one of the families of Kirjath-jearim, from yether (H3499), a remainder, that which is left over, an excess or abundance.
biblical_def: The Ithrites were one of the families of Kirjath-jearim, listed in the genealogy of Judah with the Puhites, the Shumathites and the Mishraites, of them came the Zareathites, and the Eshtaulites (1Ch 2:53). Two of David's mighty men came out of this clan: Ira an Ithrite, Gareb an Ithrite, standing side by side near the end of the roll of the thirty (2Sa 23:38; 1Ch 11:40). Kirjath-jearim was the town where the ark rested for twenty years in the house of Abinadab after the Philistines sent it back, until David came to fetch it up to Jerusalem. So the family that produced two of the king's guard came from the village that had kept the ark through Israel's low years, when all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD (1Sa 7:2). The name is built on yether, what is left over — the same word Scripture uses for a remnant. Two men out of a small clan in a half-forgotten town is exactly the arithmetic of the remnant.
webster_summary: A family of Kirjath-jearim in the genealogy of Judah; Ira and Gareb of David's mighty men were Ithrites.

corruption_summary: Small and obscure origins are taken as disqualifying; God's habit is to draw His servants out of places nobody is watching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody disputes the Ithrites. The instinct their record corrects is the one that assumes usefulness follows from advantage — the right town, the right family, the right platform. Kirjath-jearim was a border village that had ended up with the ark of God on its hands almost by accident, because the Philistines wanted rid of it and Bethshemesh was afraid of it. It kept the ark for twenty years while Israel drifted. Out of one clan in that village came two men of David's guard.

Nathanael asked Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? (Joh 1:46), and the answer was standing in front of him. God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise… and base things of the world, and things which are despised… that no flesh should glory in his presence (1Co 1:27-29). The principle to recover is that the register of God's servants is not drawn from the places that expect to supply them, and a believer in an obscure congregation in an unregarded town is standing exactly where the Bible keeps finding people.

etymology: Hebrew Adullami (H5726), an inhabitant of Adullam, a Canaanite city in the lowland of Judah; the same district in which David later took refuge in the cave of Adullam.
biblical_def: The word occurs three times, all in one chapter, and all of one man: Hirah the Adullamite, the friend of Judah. And it came to pass at that time, that Judah went down from his brethren, and turned in to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah (Gen 38:1). That single verse sets up everything that follows in the most sordid chapter in Genesis. Judah leaves his brethren, settles among Canaanites, marries a Canaanite woman, buries two wicked sons, withholds the third from Tamar, and then goes up to his sheepshearers with his friend Hirah and turns aside to a woman he takes for a harlot who is in fact his daughter in law. It is Hirah whom Judah sends back with the kid to redeem his pledge, and who cannot find her (Gen 38:20). And out of this chapter, by Tamar, comes Pharez, and from Pharez comes David, and from David comes Christ (Mat 1:3). The chapter is not an interruption of the Joseph narrative; it is the contrast to it — Joseph resisting a Egyptian woman in chapter 39, Judah yielding among Canaanites in chapter 38.
webster_summary: An inhabitant of Adullam in the lowland of Judah; in Scripture the designation of Hirah, the friend with whom Judah kept company.

And in process of time the daughter of Shuah Judah's wife died; and Judah was comforted, and went up unto his sheepshearers to Timnath, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
corruption_summary: Companionship is treated as morally neutral; Genesis 38 opens by telling us whom Judah went down to, and everything follows from it.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 38 begins with a movement and a friendship: Judah went down from his brethren and turned in to Hirah. Nothing is said against Hirah directly; he appears to be an ordinary decent neighbour who runs Judah's errand and is discreet about it. That is exactly the point. The narrative does not require a villain. It requires only that a covenant man separate himself from his brethren and settle his friendships among people with different gods, and the rest follows over twenty years — a Canaanite marriage, sons so wicked the LORD slew them, injustice to a widow, and a man soliciting what he took to be a roadside harlot with his friend standing by.

Scripture states the rule flatly: be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners (1Co 15:33), and he that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed (Pro 13:20). This is not a call to withdraw from unbelievers, for then must ye needs go out of the world (1Co 5:10); it is about the company a man makes his own. And yet the chapter ends with grace it did not earn: Tamar, wronged and desperate, bears Pharez, and Matthew puts her name in the genealogy of Christ. The principle to recover is both halves — that our friendships shape us more than we believe, and that God's purpose runs on through the wreckage we make.

etymology: Hebrew Beerothi (H886), an inhabitant of Beeroth, one of the four Gibeonite cities; from beer (H875), a well.
biblical_def: Beeroth was one of the four cities of the Gibeonites who obtained a league with Joshua by pretending to come from a far country, and it was afterwards reckoned to Benjamin. Its people are named in two very different connections. The first is a crime: the sons of Rimmon a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin — Baanah and Rechab, captains of Ishbosheth's bands — came about the heat of the day to the house of their master, who lay on a bed at noon, and murdered him in his bed, and carried his head to David at Hebron expecting a reward (2Sa 4:2, 5). David's answer was to name the deed for what it was and execute them. The second is honourable: Naharai the Beerothite, armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah, is listed among the thirty (2Sa 23:37). The same small town produced two regicides and one of the king's mighty men. The parenthesis in the record is its own quiet note: the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day (2Sa 4:3).
webster_summary: An inhabitant of Beeroth, a Gibeonite city reckoned to Benjamin; the murderers of Ishbosheth were Beerothites, and so was Naharai, armourbearer to Joab.

corruption_summary: Serving a good cause is taken to sanctify the deed; David executed the men who murdered his rival in bed and expected thanks.
corruption_paragraphs: Baanah and Rechab had read the political situation correctly. Abner was dead, Ishbosheth's cause was collapsing, David was certain to reign over all Israel, and the LORD had said so. They removed the last obstacle and brought the head to Hebron with a piece of theology attached: the LORD hath avenged my lord the king this day of Saul, and of his seed (2Sa 4:8). Every clause of their reasoning about the outcome was true. David had them killed, and told them why: when one told me, saying, Behold, Saul is dead… I took hold of him, and slew him in Ziklag… How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed? (2Sa 4:10-11).

This is the standing refusal of Scripture to let a good end launder a wicked means. Paul states it as a question and answers it with the strongest negative in the Greek: Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just (Rom 3:8). Uzzah steadied the ark with the best of intentions. Saul spared the Amalekite cattle to sacrifice them. The principle to recover is that God does not need our sins to accomplish His promises, and that a man who commits one in the service of a cause he is sure God favours has still committed it, and will answer for it.

etymology: Hebrew Qorchi (H7145), the descendants of Korah the son of Izhar, of the tribe of Levi; also written Korahites and Kohathites' kinsmen in the registers.
biblical_def: The Korhites are the family of Korah, and their existence is a standing monument to mercy. Korah led two hundred and fifty princes in rebellion against Moses and Aaron and the earth opened and swallowed him; yet Numbers records, almost in passing, notwithstanding the children of Korah died not (Num 26:11). Exodus had already named the survivors: the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these are the families of the Korhites (Exo 6:24). What became of them is the remarkable part. Korhites appear among the valiant men who came to David at Ziklag (1Ch 12:6). They served as porters, keepers of the gates of the house of God, the doorkeepers of the sanctuary their ancestor had tried to seize. They stood with the Kohathites to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high when Jehoshaphat went out against Moab and Ammon (2Ch 20:19). And eleven psalms carry their name in the title — including the psalm that says a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness (Psa 84:10).
webster_summary: The descendants of Korah the Levite, who survived his rebellion and became porters, singers and psalmists in the house of God.
webster_full: KORHITES, Hebrew Qorchi, the descendants of Korah the son of Izhar, of Levi.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah and Abiasaph.
Notwithstanding the rebellion of their father, the children of Korah died not.
Korhites were among the valiant men who came to David at Ziklag, and served as porters of the house of God.
Eleven psalms bear the title for the sons of Korah.
scriptures: Exo 6:24
And the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these are the families of the Korhites.
Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites,
And the Levites, of the children of the Kohathites, and of the children of the Korhites, stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high.
Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.
corruption_summary: A family disgraced is assumed to be finished with God; the sons of Korah ended up writing the psalms and keeping the doors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody argues about the Korhites. What their history argues against is despair — the settled conviction, common in people with a wrecked family behind them, that the name they carry has already decided what they may be. Korah's rebellion is the worst mutiny in the Pentateuch, put down by a judgment so direct that Israel fled at the cry of it. If any household in Israel had grounds for believing itself written off, it was his.

God's own footnote is the six words in Numbers 26:11 — notwithstanding the children of Korah died not — and the next eight hundred years are the commentary on it. Their sons kept the doors of the house their father had tried to storm, sang in the temple courts, and gave the church Psalms 42 and 84 and 46. Ezekiel states the doctrine: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Eze 18:20), and Paul the consequence: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away (2Co 5:17). The principle to recover is that the grace of God cuts across inheritance, and that the deepest longing a man can have — I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God — was written by the descendants of the man who wanted the priesthood by force.

etymology: Hebrew Arpad (H774), a Syrian city near Hamath in the north, commonly read as support or couch; also written Arphad.
biblical_def: Arpad was a Syrian city north of Hamath, and in Scripture it is always a name in a list of the fallen. Rabshakeh, standing outside the wall of Jerusalem with Sennacherib's army behind him, used it as his clinching argument: Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand? (2Ki 18:34). The letter Sennacherib afterwards sent to Hezekiah pressed the same point — Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad? (2Ki 19:13). Isaiah records Assyria's own boast in the same terms (Isa 10:9), and Jeremiah, generations later, names the city in a lament over Damascus: Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are fainthearted (Jer 49:23). The argument from Arpad was empirically strong and theologically worthless. Hezekiah took Sennacherib's letter into the house of the LORD and spread it before Him, and prayed; and the answer came that night.
webster_summary: A Syrian city near Hamath, named by Rabshakeh among the conquered cities whose gods could not deliver them.
webster_full: ARPAD, Hebrew Arpad, a city of Syria near Hamath; also written Arphad.
Named by Rabshakeh in his taunt before the wall of Jerusalem.
Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?
Named again in the letter of Sennacherib to Hezekiah, and in the boast recorded by Isaiah.
Jeremiah names it with Hamath as confounded and fainthearted at evil tidings.
scriptures: Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?
Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivah?
Isa 10:9
Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?
Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are fainthearted; there is sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet.
corruption_summary: The God of Israel is filed among the gods that failed; Rabshakeh's mistake was to reason from idols to the living God.
corruption_paragraphs: Rabshakeh's speech is the oldest form of the argument from religious history: your god is one of many, the others have all failed, the record is public, and there is no reason to expect a different outcome. Arpad and Hamath and Sepharvaim had gods, and those gods are gone. The reasoning is competent as far as it goes, and it is the shape of the modern version too — that Christianity takes its place in a long museum of expired deities, each of which was believed as sincerely as the next.

Hezekiah's answer is the only answer, and he made it in prayer rather than in debate: of a truth, LORD, the kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations and their lands, and have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them. Now therefore, O LORD our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the LORD God, even thou only (2Ki 19:17-19). The category is wrong: the gods of Arpad were carpentry. The LORD is not the best of a class of beings but the only one there is, and He answered that night, and Sennacherib went home and died in the house of his own god. The principle to recover is that the comparative-religion argument only works if you have already assumed its conclusion.

etymology: Hebrew Bilhan (H1092), commonly read tender or modest, related to Bilhah, the name of Rachel's handmaid.
biblical_def: Two men bear this name, one an Edomite and one an Israelite. The first is a Horite, son of Ezer, among the dukes of the land of Seir whose genealogy Moses records alongside Esau's: The children of Ezer are these; Bilhan, and Zaavan, and Akan (Gen 36:27; 1Ch 1:42). The second is a Benjamite, son of Jediael, and his household is one of the more striking notices in Chronicles: the sons also of Jediael; Bilhan: and the sons of Bilhan; Jeush, and Benjamin, and Ehud, and Chenaanah, and Zethan, and Tharshish, and Ahishahar (1Ch 7:10). Seven sons named in one verse, heads of houses among mighty men of valour, and the next verse counts the fighting men of the house at seventeen thousand two hundred. That Moses should give a chapter of Genesis to the dukes of Edom — the line of the brother who sold his birthright — is characteristic of Scripture's honesty. God keeps records of the nations He did not choose, and the Edomite genealogy is set down as carefully as Israel's.
webster_summary: The name of two men: a Horite son of Ezer among the dukes of Seir, and a Benjamite son of Jediael whose house was numerous and valiant.
webster_full: BILHAN, Hebrew Bilhan, commonly read tender or modest.
1. A Horite, son of Ezer, in the genealogy of the dukes of the land of Seir.

2. A Benjamite, son of Jediael, whose seven sons were heads of their fathers' houses.
The fighting men of that house numbered seventeen thousand and two hundred.

The sons of Ezer; Bilhan, and Zavan, and Jakan. The sons of Dishan; Uz, and Aran.
The sons also of Jediael; Bilhan: and the sons of Bilhan; Jeush, and Benjamin, and Ehud, and Chenaanah, and Zethan, and Tharshish, and Ahishahar.

The LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps an honest record of the peoples He did not choose.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bilhan is uncontested. What his double appearance illustrates is a feature of Scripture that surprises readers who expect propaganda. Genesis 36 is a long, careful, unhostile genealogy of Edom — the dukes of Esau and the dukes of the Horites — recorded by Moses in the middle of the story of Israel's election. A book written to flatter a nation does not devote a chapter to the family tree of the rival it has just displaced.

The doctrine underneath is that election is God's free choice and not a verdict on the inherent worth of the chosen. Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau (Mal 1:2-3), and Paul presses that very text to show that the purpose of God according to election stands not of works, but of him that calleth (Rom 9:11-13). Israel had no ground for boasting, and Moses told them so: the LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people (Deu 7:7). The principle to recover is humility about election. The chosen have nothing they did not receive, and the record of the unchosen is written down with the same care.
